This is the last criterion in the language rubric. Connectors, transitions, and paragraphing.
So, remember, in our rubric the organizational tools are split into three.
Connectors, transition sentences, and dividing the essay into paragraphs. The official guide names exactly these: conjunctions, transition sentences and correct paragraphing.
Let's go through them. We'll start with connectors.
So what's a connector? It's a word that tells you how the part before it and the part after it are related.
Connectors support focus and coherence. They keep the main line of thought, and they keep the reading flowing. They help the reader see how the different parts connect.
Now, notice I said the part before and the part after. That's because connectors can show up in three places.
Inside a sentence, between its first part and its second part. Agreement, detail, explanation, contrast.
Between sentences, inside the paragraph. One sentence, then the next one explains it, then the next one goes against it.
And between paragraphs. Connectors at the start of a paragraph that tell us how this paragraph relates to the one before.
Let's look at an example.
I've highlighted the connectors. We have connectors inside sentences, between sentences, and even at the start of the paragraph.
'On the other hand'. Right away I know this paragraph is going to go against the one before it. That's a connector between paragraphs.
'Some call for a ban since...' So the second part of the sentence will explain the first. Why ban them? Because they're involved in a higher share of accidents.
'Admittedly'. That's a kind of half agreement, with a reservation. 'Admittedly this figure is accurate; however'. And there's the contrast.
'Unlike accidents involving larger vehicles'. Here we have a comparison.
Now, everything I just said... comparison, detail, explanation... you really don't need to know the names of all the types of connectors.
You just need to understand the connectors you use.
If a connector is hard for you, don't use it. A lot of students see 'albeit' and think it means 'also', like an addition. It actually means 'although'.
Another classic. 'On the contrary' is not the same as 'on the other hand'. 'On the contrary' says what came before is wrong. To bring in the other side, write 'on the other hand'.
And some connectors come with grammar. 'Because' goes before a full clause. 'Because of', 'due to', 'despite' go before a noun. And 'however' starts a new sentence, or comes after a semicolon.
Now, a really important rule.
A connector signals a relationship. It doesn't create one.
Putting 'therefore' in front of a conclusion doesn't prove that it follows. I mean, why would recording streets make crime disappear? The step in the middle is missing.
Here the link is explained. So now 'as a result' describes a relationship that really exists. And notice it's 'may', not 'will disappear'.
And 'however' between two positions that contradict each other doesn't explain why there's an exception. You have to explain it. What's different about homes?
So first, figure out the relationship. Cause, result, contrast, concession, condition, example. Then pick the connector that says it accurately.
Here are the main English connectors, grouped by the relationship they show.
Cause and result, contrast and concession, condition, example, addition, and conclusion.
Concession is the one students forget. You admit part of the other side's point, and then you add your reservation. 'Admittedly... however'. 'Although this is true...'.
You don't need all of them. Two or three from each group that you really understand are plenty. You'll find this table on the card after the lesson.
Now, connectors at the start of paragraphs. Here's a list you can go through.
The opening paragraph doesn't start with a connector. It usually starts with 'In recent years' or 'Recently', depending on the background in the task.
The first argument paragraph opens with its key sentence, and the key sentence starts with 'In my opinion' or 'I believe that'. No connector needed.
The second argument paragraph adds a connector before it. 'Moreover, in my opinion', 'In addition, I believe that'. 'First, in my opinion' sounds awkward, so skip the numbers.
The rebuttal paragraph. Now I want to face the other side, there's a counter-argument. So, 'On the other hand', 'Nevertheless', 'Admittedly'. There's contrast here.
And the closing paragraph. I want to sum up. 'In conclusion', 'To sum up', 'In light of the above'.
Paragraphing, and transition sentences.
First of all, the essay is made of paragraphs. Each paragraph has a specific role, and we have to make sure each one does its job in the essay.
The paragraphs have to connect to each other and keep the line of thought. And that's where the connectors come in.
The official guide says the division into paragraphs should reflect the ideas in the essay. So, a new idea, a new paragraph.
Transition sentences are sentences that connect paragraphs, and help the reader follow the line of thought.
So I can connect paragraphs with a connector... or with a longer sentence that explains how the paragraphs relate.
The transition sentence reminds the reader where we've been, preventing crime, and tells them where we're going now. What happens after a crime.
The rule is, one argument per paragraph.
But sometimes two points come from the same field, and serve one argument. For example, two economic points. One from the employers' side, and one from the workers' side.

Take lower tax for large companies. The benefit to the companies, and the benefit to their employees. Both are economic, and together they make one argument: the economy gains. So they share one paragraph.
If the points come from different perspectives, they're different arguments, so we split them. If they're from the same field and serve one argument, I combine them.
Because if I split them into two paragraphs, they'd look too similar to each other. And that weakens the critical thinking I'm showing.
And now, how it looks on the answer sheet.
In the middle of a paragraph, we don't start a new line. Just keep writing until you finish the paragraph.
When you move to the next paragraph, it's a good idea to indent. Start a little further in, and leave that bit blank.

We also suggest leaving a blank line between paragraphs. That way you have room for corrections later, without crossing out and squeezing words above the line. Just make sure the essay still fits in the fifty lines.
